en: Can a lion be ordinary?
Lion Manas the wolf-man:
Can one prosper without seeking him?
Clear-minded Bakay, listen to my words.
Can you remain where you are?
When lion Manas was born,
He was born larger than a pale-eyed sheep;
He was born standing upright on his feet.
When the wolf-man was born,
His feet reached the ground.
Beside him, eighty-one old women
Fell flat, the poor creatures,
And departed from this world.
A dark blue mane, a stiff mane,
Rose distinct along his back.
When Manas was born,
His lion's aspect showed.
Manas, who was like that:
Can you leave him unfound?
If you fail to find Manas,
My child Bakay, listen to my words:
Will your one undertaking become two?
Let me tell you about Manas:
His form and his stature,
His appearance mounted on a horse,
With a face like oiled wheat,
With eyes like twilight mist,
Of middle height, broad-shouldered,
Wide-mouthed, with cliff-like brows,
An exceptional wrestler and a lion,
A soul companion if you find him.
Find him yourself, Bakay.
Appearing from the unseen,
These are the words I tell you.
I myself am a saint.
He is the renowned one, he is the support.
If you find Manas,
He is the lion who will be your hope.
When that blood-stained warrior appears,
Your heart will turn to him unbidden.
When you look at Manas,
He will seem closer than your father.
Such is Manas's nature.
When a storm comes, no wind reaches you;
He is a sheltered forest thicket.
He will not let an enemy take his companion;
He is a leopard, a wolf-man warrior.
Not resting upon a mountaintop,
He is a dark-mottled eagle.
Set your care upon Manas.
If you find Manas,
He is the warrior who will ease your sorrow.
My saintlike Bakay,
Find that man yourself,’
Said the wandering saint then,
And when he vanished from sight,
It was a dream as I slept;
It was God's own doing.
When I slept then,
It was Friday's Night of Power.
Who had told me of Manas
Was the saintly old man himself.
When I heard precisely this,
I yearned for his words.
‘Where is my blessed Manas?’ I asked;
I searched hard for you yourself.
What I sought has been found;
On this very day Bakay's
Honor is thus safeguarded.
Who lets no bustard escape on the gray plain,
My gray-mottled falcon,
Who never tires when ridden far,
My heroic thoroughbred, my winged steed,
O today my extinguished fire has surely kindled;
My dead soul has come alive.
God has surely granted my wish;
The one I watched for has surely come!”
Calling like a young hawk,
Gleaming in his coat of mail,
Then warrior Bakay
Before lion Manas
Came up, speaking in a ringing voice:
“O my child, I heard you came to Altay;
Shattering the people of Altay,
You entered Khangay, I heard.
Killing the khan of Khangay,
You waged a holy campaign, I heard.
Against the black Chinese and Manzhuu,
Leopard Manas arose as a warrior;
The forty households left behind
He freed, I heard.
O my child, shall I say I came from Zhelpinish?
Though I have not seen you or known you,
My wolf-man warrior, are you well?
That you, Manas, would become Manas,
I knew from the very first day.
‘When will my wolf-man emerge?’
Of Almighty God, most often,
I had been asking that.
Seven years before you were born,
I had learned news of you.
From those whose ears heard and eyes saw,
From travelers and those who stayed,
Throughout the world's four corners
I sent inquiries, having you sought.
At the earth's far end, Zhelpinish,
When I heard your accomplished name,
For seven years I searched there.
The five corners of Mediyan
I scouted, circling five times.
I suffered great hardship.
In Egypt and Baghdad
For three years I searched there.
Saddle-soring my blue-gray winged steed,
My wolf-man, on your account,
Making my heart ache terribly,
I saw a lake with no dry land.
Where not one drop of water could be found,
I saw a desert forty days across.
I traversed the whole earth;
Throughout the whole world
I wandered in my search.
Unable to find you, my accomplished one,
I scouted the face of the earth.
To Great Beijing of Kakanchyn
I went seven times.
Wandering the wide world,
Unable to find you, my exceptional one,
I endured great trouble.
I had no support to gird myself with;
My champion, I had no lion like you.
The blue-gray winged steed beneath me,
While I failed to find you in so many lands,
Had only a spoonful of blood left;
His flesh was nothing but blue lean meat.
Unable to find you, my lion,
My horse became thin as a cotoneaster twig;
My lice grew as large as larks.
My hooves had become chipped.
My falcon, now that I have found you,
My beak has now grown whole!
You are my support, my strength;
You are my lion who will brighten my brow.
Who will save my life,
You are a ravine thick with meadowsweet.
If enemies come against me and surround me,
To draw from the sheath with a shout,
You are steel fitted and ready!”
Mighty Bakay said these words:
“Turn toward the words I speak;
I will become your faithful companion.
Making you know what you do not know,
With knowledge I will set you on the path.
Making you perceive what you do not perceive,
I will bring you to understanding.
I shall lead you with me and make you a hero,
Make you the equal of a hero's son.
By kneading, I shall make you a house;
By planting, I shall make you an orchard.
If you ask what I am like:
I am a ridge rising high,
I am an utterly fierce-maned lion.
The one a fortunate man will find—
I am your princely elder Bakai.
Upon my wrist, Achbolot—
I am Bakai who hung it there.
The whole world like little birds—
I am Bakai who drove it before him.
My name is Bakai; I am an elder.
I have come from afar, roaming about.
If you heed my words, my Manas,
I have a line to draw,
Many upheavals I could set in motion.”
So spoke great Bakai.
A traveling cauldron with golden handles,
Beside the lion-hero,
Bakai brought and hung up.
They slaughtered a white-gray mare
And ate their fill of pure white fat.
A white Quran as large as a horse's head
They brought out then
And held against their breasts.
As sharers of their gains in this world,
Their bond had now reached fullness;
As brothers in faith for the next world,
They now stood united.
The white Quran, large as a horse's head,
They set between them, they say.
Magnanimous Manas and Bakai
Embraced each other, they say.
Then Manas said:
“Encountered through the unseen,
My khan and elder, there is no hero like you.
For lifting one's brow and taking joy,
There is no land like broad Talas.
Until I go to the other world,
Until this precious life, worn down,
Comes to the dust,
Turn my steed's head for me.
My hawk-like elder, hero Bakai,
Be a father to me;
Stand as my support.
The two reins and one leading rope—
Take the rule of the people.
Me, a spoiled and unruly fellow,
Contrive to set upon the path.
Bakai the hawk, my khan and elder,
Be a steadfast presence for me.
The black-cheeked battle-axe—
Fit its handle so it will not tilt.
Of the Kazakhs and Kyrgyz,
Lead the way yourself.
Take unity in hand;
Set us on the road you know.
Come and settle in Talas,
Fortunate elder Bakai.
Against the Chinese I shall do battle:
Be my steadfast companion!
Placed before me, you bring good fortune:
You are my lion Bakai.
Placed behind me, you bring good fortune:
You are my hero Bakai.
Recognizing Talas as the land for us,
Go up and settle there.
The champion of the forty chosen men—
Be Bakai, favored by Khizir.
Whose blessing enriches the people—
Be like a prophet!
You are my Bakai, my lion;
You have appeared as my refuge,
My hero who is like a prophet.”
When Manas said this,
Bakai, his khan and elder, agreed.
They ate bread of white wheat
And together held the holy Quran.
Their sheep came to share a pen;
Their meals became shared feasts.
In this world, sharers of their gains;
In the next world, brothers in faith.
Like flour of white wheat,
They were kneaded together.
Like the hairs of a white saiga,
They became the closest of friends.
For Manas, visited by Khizir,
The champion Bakai had been found.
For Manas, visited by the chilten,
A valiant man like himself had appeared.
They embraced and became friends,
Lying in the open steppe.
Your elder Bakai, the tiger—
His tales comforted the soul;
His deeds delighted the soul.
His words were sweet and sorrowful;
Such a person is not met again.
Your dear elder Bakai
Found the word at an unexpected moment;
